title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E420 recasts the calculus of variations in Euler's new 'variation' formalism. For Z = Z(x,y,p,q) with p = dy/dx and q = dp/dx, dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq, and the extremal equation for ∫Z dx is 0 = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx². The page finishes the illustrative example begun on p. 68: the elastic curve, characterized as making ∫ds/ρ² a minimum. With ρ = (1+p²)^{3/2}/q this gives Z = q²/(1+p²)^{5/2}, so M = N = 0, P = −5pq²/(1+p²)^{7/2} and Q = 2q/(1+p²)^{5/2}.

Step 1 (translation in y). Since N = 0, the equation is d/dx(P − dQ/dx) = 0. Hence P − dQ/dx = A, which is still of third order because Q contains q.

Step 2 (translation in x). Multiply by q dx = dp to get P dp − q dQ = A dp. Since Z depends only on p and q, dZ = P dp + Q dq. Substituting P dp = dZ − Q dq gives dZ − Q dq − q dQ = A dp, which integrates to Z − Qq = Ap + B. In modern terms this is the 'energy' (Hamiltonian, Noether) first integral of a second-order Lagrangian independent of x: Z − p(P − Q') − qQ = const, with P − Q' = A.

Step 3 (specialization). Here Z − qQ = −q²/(1+p²)^{5/2}. Changing the signs of the constants gives q² = (Ap+B)(1+p²)^{5/2}, so q = dp/dx = (1+p²)^{5/4}√(Ap+B). Therefore dx = dp/[(1+p²)^{5/4}√(Ap+B)] and dy = p dx, and the curve is constructed by quadratures in the slope p.

Check in angle form. Put p = tanθ. The curvature is κ = q/(1+p²)^{3/2}, so κ² = (Ap+B)/√(1+p²) = A sinθ + B cosθ = R cos(θ − θ₀). Equivalently dx = cosθ dθ/√(A sinθ + B cosθ) and ds = dθ/κ.
errors: Printed misprint: after multiplying P − dQ/dx = A by q dx = dp the right side should be A dp, not 'A dq'. Euler's next line correctly has A dp, so the slip does not propagate.

Conceptual gap: no length (isoperimetric) constraint is imposed. Varying y with fixed abscissae therefore lets the arc length vary freely, and the solutions obey κ² = R cos(θ − θ₀) with no additive constant. That is only the rectangular elastica (the 'free' elastica), not the full family of Euler's 1744 elastic curves. The general family needs ∫(1/ρ² + α) ds, i.e. a multiplier for fixed length, which Euler only discusses on the next page (§55) for isoperimetric problems in general. Calling the result 'the elastic curves' in general is therefore imprecise.
Minor: taking the square root silently selects a branch, and the sign change of the constants requires Ap + B ≥ 0 on the arc; both are harmless.

ideas.what: First integral P − dQ/dx = const for a second-order Lagrangian independent of y.
ideas.modern_name: Conserved momentum (Noether, translation in y) for higher-order Lagrangians
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744); Noether 1918 for the general principle
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744), chapters on reductions/integrable cases

ideas.what: Second first integral Z − Qq = Ap + B, obtained by multiplying by dp and using dZ = P dp + Q dq.
ideas.modern_name: Energy / Hamiltonian first integral (Ostrogradsky-type) for x-independent second-order Lagrangians
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 for the elastica); Ostrogradsky 1850 for the general higher-order Hamiltonian
ideas.where_published: E65, Additamentum I (De curvis elasticis) and the integrability cases in the main text

ideas.what: Elastica characterized as an extremal of ∫ds/ρ² and integrated by quadratures in the slope p.
ideas.modern_name: Euler elastica; the free-length case is the rectangular elastica
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli (variational principle, letter of 1742) and Euler (1744)

missed.claim: Without the length constraint, the example yields only the rectangular (free) elastica, κ² = A sinθ + B cosθ, rather than the general elastic curve. Euler does not remark on this. The fact that free elasticae are exactly rectangular elasticae is well known today (e.g. in the modern elastica literature on curve-straightening); only the observation that this 1772 example implicitly produces just that case may be uncommented.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical interest: a precise identification of which elastica Euler actually obtains here. There is no new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard worked example that repeats Euler's 1744 treatment of the elastica, here in the variation formalism. Both first integrals are classical. The only points of note are a misprint ('A dq' for 'A dp') and the unstated restriction to the free-length (rectangular) elastica.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces the printed 'P dp − q dQ = A dq'. The print itself is in error: this should read A dp.
The exponents 5:4 in q = (1+pp)^{5:4}√(Ap+B) and 5/4 in dx and dy match the image; no correction is needed.
